lead: OFDM splits one high-rate data stream into many low-rate streams, each on its own closely spaced subcarrier. The subcarriers are orthogonal over one symbol, so they overlap in frequency without interfering. An IFFT builds the transmitted symbol and an FFT separates the subcarriers at the receiver. A cyclic prefix absorbs delay spread, making a frequency-selective channel look flat on each subcarrier. OFDM is the base of LTE and Wi-Fi, where it is called OFDMA when subcarriers are shared among users.
prereq: You need: QPSK and M-ary PSK, M-ary QAM, ISI and the Nyquist criterion from Unit 5, and random processes from Unit 1.

sections.h3: One wide band becomes many narrow bands

blocks.text: A high-rate single carrier over a multipath channel has a symbol time shorter than the delay spread. Echoes from buildings and hills then smear one symbol into the next, giving intersymbol interference (ISI). A wideband equalizer can undo this, but it is complex. OFDM takes another route: it sends N low-rate streams in parallel, one on each subcarrier. Each stream has a long useful symbol duration T_u, so the same delay spread is a small fraction of a symbol. The subcarriers are spaced by Δf = 1/T_u and are orthogonal over T_u, so their spectra may overlap without cross-talk. N subcarriers occupy about N Δf hertz. A 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel can carry 64 subcarriers at 312.5 kHz spacing, each much narrower than the channel's coherence bandwidth.

blocks.where: Δf is the subcarrier spacing in hertz; T_u is the useful OFDM symbol duration in seconds; N is the number of subcarriers.

sections.h3: IFFT at the transmitter, FFT at the receiver

blocks.text: The transmitter first maps bits to complex QAM symbols. For one OFDM symbol it collects N such symbols, X[0] to X[N−1], one per subcarrier. An inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) turns these frequency-domain values into N time samples. The receiver applies a fast Fourier transform (FFT) to return to the frequency domain. The FFT is efficient: N log₂ N operations instead of N² for a direct transform.

items: Map incoming bits to X[k] using QPSK or QAM; k = 0, 1, ..., N−1.
Compute x[n] by an N-point IFFT of X[k].
Copy the last G time samples to the front as the cyclic prefix; send the N+G samples.
At the receiver, discard the first G samples and take an N-point FFT to get Y[k].
Multiply Y[k] by 1/H[k] to undo the channel on subcarrier k; then QAM-demap.

blocks.text: x[n] = (1/N) Σₖ₌₀ᴺ⁻¹ X[k] e^(j2πkn/N),  n = 0, ..., N−1
blocks.where: x[n] is the nth time sample; X[k] is the complex QAM symbol on subcarrier k; N is the number of subcarriers; j = √−1.
Y[k] is the received value on subcarrier k; H[k] is the channel gain on subcarrier k; W[k] is noise on subcarrier k.

blocks.text: After the cyclic prefix is removed, the channel acts as a circular convolution. The FFT turns that into a multiplication on each subcarrier: Y[k] = H[k]X[k] + W[k]. The equalizer is therefore one complex multiply per subcarrier, not a long filter. This is the main reason OFDM is cheap in the receiver.

sections.h3: Cyclic prefix, delay spread and fading

blocks.text: The cyclic prefix (CP) is a copy of the tail of the IFFT output placed before it. It costs extra time but protects the useful symbol. Let G be the CP length in samples and T_s = 1/(N Δf) the sample time. Then T_cp = G T_s and the total symbol time is T = T_u + T_cp. The rule is T_cp > τ_max, where τ_max is the maximum channel delay spread. If this holds, echoes from the previous symbol die inside the CP; after CP removal there is no ISI. If T_cp is too short, ISI and intercarrier interference (ICI) appear.

blocks.where: T is the total OFDM symbol time in seconds; T_u is the useful symbol duration; T_cp is the cyclic prefix duration.

blocks.text: OFDM does not delete fading. It changes its shape. A channel is flat if its coherence bandwidth B_c is much larger than the signal bandwidth; all frequencies have nearly the same gain. It is frequency-selective if B_c is smaller than the signal bandwidth; different frequencies fade differently. In OFDM the whole signal may be frequency-selective, but each subcarrier is narrow, so each subcarrier sees almost flat fading and gets one equalizer gain H[k].

Slow and fast fading use time. Coherence time T_c is the time over which the channel stays roughly constant. If T_c is much larger than the OFDM symbol T, fading is slow: H[k] changes over many symbols. If T_c is comparable to or smaller than T, fading is fast and channel estimates go stale. Doppler spread f_d = v f_c / c sets T_c roughly as 1/f_d, where v is speed, f_c is carrier frequency and c is the speed of light. Only a few syllabi treat fading in detail; the exam usually asks for these names and the CP rule.

sections.h3: Practical problems and where OFDM is used

blocks.text: Two practical problems dominate. First, the peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR): many subcarriers adding in phase can give a large peak, so the power amplifier must back off and loses efficiency. Second, synchronisation: the receiver must align its FFT window and carrier frequency; a small frequency error breaks orthogonality and causes ICI. Channel estimation is also needed to find H[k].

items: OFDMA shares groups of subcarriers among users; LTE downlink uses it.
Wi-Fi uses OFDM in its high-rate physical layers.
The CP is overhead: raw bit rate must use T, not T_u.

figure.caption: The IFFT and FFT pair is the core of the link; the cyclic prefix is inserted before the fading channel and removed after it. Notice that the only channel correction shown is after the FFT, where it can be one gain per subcarrier.

spec.title: OFDM link
spec.aria: Data is QAM mapped, passed through an IFFT, cyclic prefix added, sent over a fading channel, cyclic prefix removed, FFT processed, QAM demapped and thresholded.

examples.question: An OFDM system uses 64 subcarriers in 20 MHz, a 16-sample cyclic prefix, and 64-QAM on every subcarrier. Find the subcarrier spacing, useful symbol duration, cyclic prefix duration, total symbol duration, and uncoded bit rate.
steps: Subcarrier spacing: Δf = B/N = 20 MHz / 64 = 0.3125 MHz = 312.5 kHz.
Useful symbol duration: T_u = 1/Δf = 1/(312.5 kHz) = 3.2 μs.
Cyclic prefix duration: T_cp = 16 × T_s = 16 × 50 ns = 800 ns = 0.8 μs.
Total symbol duration: T = T_u + T_cp = 3.2 μs + 0.8 μs = 4.0 μs.
64-QAM carries log₂ 64 = 6 bits per subcarrier. Bits per OFDM symbol = 64 × 6 = 384 bits.
Uncoded bit rate: R_b = 384 bits / 4.0 μs = 96 × 10⁶ bit/s = 96 Mbps.
examples.answer: The system has Δf = 312.5 kHz, T_u = 3.2 μs, T_cp = 0.8 μs, T = 4.0 μs, and an uncoded bit rate of 96 Mbps.
examples.check:
import math
B = 20e6
N = 64
G = 16
M = 64
delta_f = B/N
T_u = 1/delta_f
T_s = 1/B
T_cp = G*T_s
T = T_u + T_cp
bits_per_sc = int(math.log2(M))
R_b = N*bits_per_sc/T
print(delta_f/1e3)
print(T_u*1e6)
print(T_cp*1e6)
print(T*1e6)
print(R_b/1e6)

traps: Using T_u instead of T = T_u + T_cp in the bit-rate calculation; the cyclic prefix is overhead and lowers the raw rate.
Saying OFDM removes fading. It removes ISI when the CP is long enough; fading remains as a flat gain H[k] on each subcarrier.
Confusing subcarrier spacing with the total symbol rate. Δf = 1/T_u, but the transmitted OFDM symbol lasts T = T_u + T_cp.
Making the cyclic prefix shorter than the channel delay spread. The CP must be longer than τ_max to avoid ISI and ICI.
Forgetting the factor N or log₂ M in bits per OFDM symbol: bits per symbol = N log₂ M for M-QAM on every subcarrier.

quiz.q: What is the role of the IFFT in an OFDM transmitter?
quiz.a: It converts N complex QAM symbols, one per subcarrier, into N time samples of one OFDM symbol.

quiz.q: Why can OFDM subcarriers overlap in frequency without interfering?
quiz.a: They are spaced by Δf = 1/T_u and are orthogonal over T_u, so the integral of one subcarrier times the complex conjugate of another is zero over one useful symbol.

quiz.q: An OFDM system has subcarrier spacing 15 kHz and a cyclic prefix equal to 10% of T_u. Find T_u, T_cp and T.
A 20 MHz OFDM system uses 64 subcarriers and a 16-sample CP. With QPSK on every subcarrier, find the uncoded bit rate.
quiz.a: Δf = 20 MHz/64 = 312.5 kHz, so T_u = 3.2 μs. T_s = 50 ns, so T_cp = 0.8 μs and T = 4.0 μs. QPSK gives 2 bits per subcarrier, so bits per symbol = 64 × 2 = 128. R_b = 128/4.0 μs = 32 Mbps.

quiz.q: Explain why a frequency-selective channel becomes many flat subchannels in OFDM, and what the CP does.
quiz.a: Each subcarrier is narrow compared with the channel coherence bandwidth, so its gain is almost constant and is just H[k]. The CP makes the channel look like a circular convolution and keeps echoes inside the prefix, so the FFT gives Y[k] = H[k]X[k] + W[k] and one complex multiply equalizes each subcarrier.

quiz.q: What happens if T_cp is shorter than the maximum delay spread τ_max? Name two impairments.
quiz.a: Energy from the previous OFDM symbol enters the current symbol, causing ISI. The subcarriers also lose orthogonality, causing intercarrier interference (ICI).

quiz.q: Distinguish flat and frequency-selective fading using coherence bandwidth.
quiz.a: Flat fading has coherence bandwidth much larger than the signal bandwidth, so all frequencies see nearly the same gain. Frequency-selective fading has coherence bandwidth smaller than the signal bandwidth, so different frequencies fade differently.

quiz.q: State two practical problems of OFDM.
quiz.a: High peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) and sensitivity to carrier-frequency and timing synchronisation errors.

beyond: Not for the exam. 5G NR keeps CP-OFDM for wideband data and adds DFT-s-OFDM for uplink coverage. Wi-Fi 6 and 7 use OFDM with multi-user scheduling. Research work goes into PAPR reduction, better channel estimation, MIMO-OFDM and OTFS for high Doppler. Search terms: OFDMA resource grid, PAPR reduction, pilot-based channel estimation, MIMO-OFDM.
